headline: Wiles quit after the midterms. Miller is chief of staff.
summary: Susie Wiles resigned as White House chief of staff on Thursday night, two days after Republicans lost both houses of Congress. On Friday Trump named Stephen Miller, 41, the architect of his hardline immigration policy, to replace her from Monday. Last month Trump said there was "zero chance" she would go. She was the first woman in the job.
cover_answer: No. She quit, two days after his side lost the vote.
table_question: If your team loses, who should take the blame?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president has a helper who runs his office, the way a head teacher runs a school. Her name is Susie Wiles, and she quit this week after the president's team lost a big vote. A man named Stephen Miller takes her job on Monday, like a new teacher taking over a class in the middle of the year. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: One helper out, one in, a school they know. At seven the job is the head teacher and the election is a game their team lost.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the job becomes a head teacher and the change is one person leaving and one arriving on Monday. The lost election is a lost game, the only version of blame this age can use. Expect "was she bad?" The president said she did a very good job. Then he said moves have to be made.

8-12.script: On Tuesday the president's party lost both halves of Congress. Thursday night his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, resigned; Axios reports Trump blamed her. Friday he gave the job to Stephen Miller, who wrote his toughest immigration rules. A coach loses the final and swaps in the hardest assistant on the bench.
8-12.why: Loss, blame, replacement: a chain. The coach is a fairness call at 12.
8-12.why_long: At this age they are working out whether blame lands where it should, so the script hands over the chain: a lost election, a resignation two days later, a replacement who wrote the rejected policies. The coach swapping assistants is a fairness call they make on their own. Expect "was it her fault?" Trump blamed her, Axios says.

13-17.script: Axios says the hardline policies Stephen Miller wrote helped Republicans lose Congress on Tuesday. Trump's answer, Friday: put Miller in charge of the White House. Defiance or conviction, and does it matter which? Second: a month ago Trump said "zero chance" Wiles would go. What is that worth?
13-17.why: A voters' verdict, and a president who answered with Miller. Hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: voters rebuked the hardline agenda on Tuesday, and on Friday its author got the top job. The script asks whether that is defiance or conviction and lets them say. Expect "doesn't he have to listen to the vote?" No law says so. Then ask what a 'zero chance' promise is worth four weeks later.

5-7.a: No. She quit, two days after his team lost a big vote. He said she did a very good job.

8-12.q: Why quit if she did a good job?
8-12.a: The party lost. Axios says Trump blamed her, not himself.

8-12.q: What does a chief of staff do?
8-12.a: Runs the White House staff. The BBC calls her one of its most powerful figures.

13-17.q: Isn't this the opposite of the vote?
13-17.a: Democrats say so. A Republican, Rep. Stutzman, called it 'horrible'.
Yes, 'zero chance', last month. Now he says moves have to be made.
